(CNN) -- The September issue of Essence magazine features an interview with Sen. Barack Obama and his family inside their Chicago home. Angela Burt-Murray is editor-in-chief of Essence magazine. Essence editor-in-chief Angela Burt-Murray said it took a year for the magazine to gain access to the Obama's Illinois home for an intimate interview with the presumptive Democratic presidential nominee, his wife, Michelle, and their daughters, Sasha and Malia. Burt-Murray talked Thursday with CNN "American Morning" anchor Kiran Chetry about the interview and the Obama family. Chetry: You are the first African-American media outlet to get this inside look. Did your team get a chance to see the real Obamas? Burt-Murray: I think we did. We went to their home on the South Side of Chicago and it was wonderful to see them as a family interacting with each other, and see the girls skipping around the house, just acting like it's a normal, everyday occurrence to have a camera crew in their home and Secret Service at different points throughout the house and around the yard. But it didn't really seem to impact the girls in any way.  Watch what Essence found inside the Obamas' home » . Chetry: Much was made of an earlier televised interview they with their daughters and they said, looking back, they probably shouldn't have done that. There is so much interest about their family, and yet they want to protect their girls. How do they balance that? Burt-Murray: They try to take a look at who is around the family and make sure they try to keep things as structured as possible. But also, you have instances where magazines like Essence show up to take photographs, but the girls are very relaxed because they're in their home environment. And I think that's the difference between our photo shoot and what you saw on television. Taking the girls outside of their home and putting them in the spotlight is probably a bit more challenging for them as parents. Chetry: They have to deal with completing stereotypes, if you will: They were parodied as these angry black radicals and as these Ivy League elitists. In the magazine, Gwen Ifill wrote, "The Obamas pride themselves on creating a family picture that is authentically black with shades of Norman Rockwell." Explain that. How are they getting that image out. Burt-Murray: I think it's the idea that they're just an average American family. They have strong family values, they're deeply rooted in their community and they want to show their girls a great example of achievement. But they also want to be a model for the rest of their community. The Obamas talk about in our story how important it is for them to continue to live in their South Side Chicago neighborhood because it's a neighborhood in transition. So you have children who have the opportunity to see an African-American man run for the highest office in the nation right in their neighborhood. So they're modeling not only for their children but also for the larger community. Chetry: They do live in a gated community, a $1.6 million home, so it's out of reach for a lot of people. Burt-Murray: But it's so accessible. While we were there photographing them for Essence, you could see the cars going by and stopping and people getting out to take photographs. The girls were on the porch and people could see them. There is some normalcy there, but it's also obviously something very special and different. Chetry: They said race had been prominent on the campaign trail. Barack Obama told Gwen Ifill that he thinks race is a national obsession. He thinks the racial divide is not as big an issue in this country as it's made out to be. Burt-Murray: As evidenced by the success that he's had with his campaign, you can certainly see that attitudes are shifting. But there are still challenges, obviously, that need to be addressed. And it keeps coming up throughout the campaign. So it will be interesting to see what happens when the country goes to the polls in November.

outputs.L1:
(CNN) — The September issue of *Essence* magazine features an interview with Sen. Barack Obama and his family in their Chicago home.

Angela Burt-Murray, editor-in-chief of *Essence*, said it took a year for the magazine to gain access to the Obamas’ Illinois residence for an intimate interview with the presumptive Democratic presidential nominee, his wife, Michelle, and their daughters, Sasha and Malia.

On Thursday, Burt-Murray spoke with CNN’s *American Morning* anchor Kiran Chetry about the interview and the Obama family.

**Chetry:** You are the first African-American media outlet to get this inside look. Did your team have a chance to see the real Obamas?

**Burt-Murray:** I think we did. We went to their home on the South Side of Chicago, and it was wonderful to see them interacting as a family and to watch the girls skipping around the house, behaving as though having a camera crew in their home—and Secret Service agents stationed at various points throughout the house and around the yard—were a normal, everyday occurrence. It did not seem to affect the girls in any way.

*Watch what Essence found inside the Obamas’ home »*

**Chetry:** Much was made of an earlier televised interview with their daughters, and they later said they probably should not have done it. There is so much interest in their family, yet they also want to protect their girls. How do they balance that?

**Burt-Murray:** They carefully consider who is around the family and try to keep things as structured as possible. At the same time, there are occasions when magazines such as *Essence* arrive to take photographs. The girls were very relaxed because they were in their home environment, and I think that is the difference between our photo shoot and what viewers saw on television. Taking the girls out of their home and placing them in the spotlight is probably more challenging for the Obamas as parents.

**Chetry:** They have had to contend with competing stereotypes, if you will: They have been parodied both as angry Black radicals and as Ivy League elitists. In the magazine, Gwen Ifill wrote, “The Obamas pride themselves on creating a family picture that is authentically black with shades of Norman Rockwell.” Explain that. How are they conveying that image?

**Burt-Murray:** I think it is the idea that they are simply an average American family. They have strong family values, are deeply rooted in their community and want to provide their daughters with a powerful example of achievement. They also want to serve as a model for the rest of their community.

In our story, the Obamas discuss how important it is for them to continue living in their South Side Chicago neighborhood because it is a community in transition. Children there have the opportunity to see an African-American man from their own neighborhood run for the nation’s highest office. The Obamas are therefore serving as role models not only for their own children, but also for the broader community.

**Chetry:** They do live in a gated community, in a $1.6 million home, so that lifestyle is beyond the reach of many people.

**Burt-Murray:** But it is still very accessible. While we were there photographing them for *Essence*, we could see cars passing by and stopping, with people getting out to take pictures. The girls were on the porch, where people could see them. There is a sense of normalcy, but it is also clearly something very special and different.

**Chetry:** They said race had been prominent on the campaign trail. Barack Obama told Gwen Ifill that he believes race is a national obsession. He also thinks the racial divide in this country is not as significant an issue as it is often portrayed.

**Burt-Murray:** The success of his campaign certainly demonstrates that attitudes are shifting. However, there are still obvious challenges that must be addressed, and the issue continues to surface throughout the campaign. It will be interesting to see what happens when the country goes to the polls in November.
outputs.L2:
(CNN) — Essence magazine’s September edition includes a profile of Sen. Barack Obama and his family, based on an interview conducted at their Chicago residence.

Angela Burt-Murray, the magazine’s editor-in-chief, said Essence spent a year securing permission for a personal visit with the presumptive Democratic presidential nominee, his wife, Michelle, and their daughters, Sasha and Malia, at the family’s Illinois home.

On Thursday, Burt-Murray discussed the article and the Obama family with Kiran Chetry, an anchor on CNN’s “American Morning.”

Chetry noted that Essence was the first Black media organization invited to offer such a close view of the family and asked whether the magazine’s staff saw the Obamas as they truly are.

Burt-Murray said she believed they did. The team visited the family’s house on Chicago’s South Side and watched them interact naturally. Sasha and Malia skipped through the rooms as though having a camera crew inside—and Secret Service agents stationed in parts of the home and yard—were entirely ordinary. The security presence did not appear to affect the girls.

Chetry then referred to a previous television appearance featuring the Obama daughters, which their parents later said they probably should not have allowed. She asked how the couple managed the intense public curiosity about their family while also trying to shield their children.

According to Burt-Murray, the Obamas carefully monitor who has access to the family and work to preserve as much structure as possible. Although an Essence photography crew was present, the girls remained at ease because the session took place in familiar surroundings. She said that distinguished the magazine shoot from the televised interview: bringing the children away from home and placing them directly before the public likely creates a more difficult parenting situation.

Chetry also raised two competing stereotypes the Obamas had confronted: portrayals of them as angry Black radicals and, alternatively, as privileged Ivy League elitists. She cited Gwen Ifill’s line in Essence that the family takes pride in presenting an image that is “authentically black with shades of Norman Rockwell,” and asked how they communicated that identity.

Burt-Murray explained that the Obamas sought to be seen as an ordinary American household with firm family principles, deep community ties, and a desire to give their daughters an inspiring example of accomplishment. At the same time, they hoped to serve as role models beyond their own family.

In the article, the Obamas emphasized the importance of remaining in their South Side neighborhood because the area was undergoing change. Their presence allowed local children to see, in their own community, an African-American man campaigning for the nation’s highest office. In that sense, Burt-Murray said, the couple was setting an example both for Sasha and Malia and for the broader neighborhood.

Chetry pointed out that the family lived in a gated community in a house valued at $1.6 million, a lifestyle beyond the reach of many Americans.

Burt-Murray responded that the family nevertheless remained visible and approachable. During the Essence photo session, passing motorists stopped their cars, got out, and took pictures. People could also see the girls standing on the porch. She said the scene retained an element of everyday life, even though the circumstances were plainly unusual and significant.

Finally, Chetry observed that race had become a major subject during the campaign. Barack Obama told Ifill that race was a national fixation and that the country’s racial separation was not as severe as it was often portrayed.

Burt-Murray said Obama’s campaign success demonstrated that public attitudes were changing, though important problems still remained. Because racial issues repeatedly surfaced during the campaign, she added, the outcome when Americans voted in November would be especially revealing.

After a year of seeking access, *Essence* magazine secured an intimate interview with Barack Obama and his family at their Chicago home. Editor-in-chief Angela Burt-Murray said the visit offered a rare opportunity to observe the Obamas interacting naturally in a familiar setting.

Despite the presence of a camera crew and Secret Service personnel, Sasha and Malia appeared relaxed and at ease. Burt-Murray noted that Barack and Michelle Obama make a deliberate effort to protect their daughters by maintaining a structured family life and carefully controlling who has access to them.

She also suggested that the girls were more comfortable being photographed in their own home than they might have been during a televised appearance elsewhere. The familiar environment allowed the family’s close, everyday dynamic to emerge more naturally.

For an entire year, *Essence* magazine worked to arrange an unusually intimate interview and photo shoot with Barack and Michelle Obama and their daughters, Malia and Sasha. Rather than meeting the family at a campaign event or in a formal studio, the magazine was invited into the Obamas’ Chicago home, where the goal was to show readers a side of the family rarely visible in public.

Inside the house, the atmosphere offered a revealing contrast to the intense attention surrounding Barack Obama’s political career. Cameras and Secret Service agents were present, but Sasha and Malia remained relaxed and behaved like children in familiar surroundings. Their natural interactions with their parents helped illustrate the family’s warmth and everyday rhythms beyond speeches, rallies, and public appearances.

The setting was especially important to Barack and Michelle Obama. At home, they could create clear boundaries and maintain a structured environment for their daughters, even as public curiosity about the family continued to grow. Familiar routines and parental expectations gave Malia and Sasha a sense of stability that the demands of politics might otherwise have disrupted.

The visit ultimately portrayed the Obama household as both ordinary and exceptional: ordinary in its affection, discipline, and family routines, yet exceptional because those routines unfolded under constant media attention and security. By allowing the interview and photographs to take place at home, the Obamas offered a carefully controlled glimpse into their private lives while demonstrating how they sought to balance public interest with their responsibility to protect their children.
